spark.summary: A feature store is a dual-plane ML data platform that computes, versions, and serves consistent features across both batch model training (offline) and low-latency real-time inference (online).
spark.keyTakeaway: By sharing one transformation definition between an offline columnar lakehouse and an online key-value store, feature stores eliminate training-serving skew and prevent accidental future data leakage.
spark.byteSummary:
**Core Mechanics:** Most production ML failures stem not from model architectures, but from **training-serving skew** (Pandas/SQL in notebooks vs. re-implemented Java/Redis in production) and **data leakage**.

**Visual & Structural Flow:** Depicts Unified Feature Registry -> Offline Lakehouse + Online KV Store (Kafka + Flink -> Online Store (Redis) -> Inference Service -> Offline Iceberg/BQ); Streaming Materialization & Guarded Inference Lookup (Kafka Events -> Flink / Spark -> Redis Online -> Inference Pod).

**Trade-Offs & Production:** Teams choose between full dual-plane platforms, lightweight DIY lookups, and request-time on-demand transforms. Production inference services pair a **1–5s in-process LRU cache** in front of the Online Store (to absorb hot-key bursts) with explicit **schema default values** for cold-start.

**Failure Modes & Application:** Explore how real-time lakehouse pipelines, hot-key caching, and Kappa streaming power production ML feature platforms.

learningJourney.title: What is an ML Feature Store
learningJourney.explanation:
Most production ML failures stem not from model architectures, but from **training-serving skew** (Pandas/SQL in notebooks vs. re-implemented Java/Redis in production) and **data leakage**. A **Feature Store** (Feast, Tecton, Hopsworks) centralizes feature definitions in a declarative registry and materializes them into two synchronized planes:

1. **Offline Store** (Iceberg, BigQuery, Snowflake): Holds years of append-only feature history for **point-in-time (AS-OF)** training joins.
2. **Online Store** (Redis, DynamoDB, Cassandra): Holds only the *latest* feature vector per entity key (`user_id`, `card_id`) for `<10 ms` real-time inference.

learningJourney.title: Why Training-Serving Skew and Data Leakage Break Models
learningJourney.explanation: Joining trip-request logs with daily driver-rating tables using `date = trip_date` leaks future ratings from later that afternoon into morning training rows—inflating offline AUC while failing in production. Similarly, subtle null-handling or timezone differences between training SQL and serving code silently degrade live predictions.

benefits: Combines 90-day batch spend profiles with 5-minute streaming velocity counts in one vector lookup.
costs: Requires Flink streaming state and high-IOPS Redis/DynamoDB clusters.

benefits: Eliminates duplicate ETL pipelines across dozens of ML teams.
costs: Needs strict schema governance and freshness SLA monitoring.

comparison.choice: Avoid: Pure Batch Scoring or Raw Unstructured LLMs
benefits: Nightly BigQuery/Spark jobs or raw text embeddings need zero online KV feature store.
costs: Maintaining Redis/Flink for batch-only churn models wastes 5x–10x infrastructure spend.

learningJourney.title: Point-in-Time AS-OF Joins & Online Freshness Guards
learningJourney.explanation: Two operational rules keep feature stores healthy: (1) use **AS-OF joins** with a bounded TTL (`ttl=90d`) for offline training, and (2) write historical backfills **strictly to the Offline Store** with timestamp-guarded conditional writes (`event_ts > current_ts`) on the Online Store so late backfills never overwrite fresher live data.
learningJourney.markdownContent:
```sql
-- Point-in-time (AS-OF) join preventing future data leakage in training sets
SELECT
  e.event_id,
  e.user_id,
  e.label_is_fraud,
  f.tx_count_last_5m,
  f.avg_spend_30d
FROM labeled_transactions e
ASOF JOIN user_velocity_features f
  MATCH_CONDITION (e.event_ts >= f.feature_ts)
  ON e.user_id = f.user_id
WHERE f.feature_ts >= DATEADD(day, -30, e.event_ts);
```

learningJourney.title: Alternatives: Managed Feature Store vs. DIY Warehouse + Redis vs. On-Demand
learningJourney.explanation: Teams choose between full dual-plane platforms, lightweight DIY lookups, and request-time on-demand transforms.

benefits: Guarantees training/serving parity, AS-OF joins, and unified feature discovery.
costs: Syncing lakehouse + Redis/DynamoDB + Flink increases operational surface.

benefits: Minimal new tooling for a single team with 5–10 features.
costs: High risk of training-serving skew and manual AS-OF join bugs.

benefits: Incorporates live request context (e.g., `distance_from_home`) impossible to precompute.
costs: Heavy aggregations cannot run at request time without blowing the 10 ms budget.

knowledgeCheck.question: During a historical feature backfill, old feature values from 30 days ago accidentally overwrite today's live values in the Online Redis Store. How do you prevent this?

options.text: Write historical backfills strictly to the Offline Store and guard Online writes with timestamp checks (`new_ts > current_ts`)
options.feedback: Correct: backfills belong in the Offline Store, and conditional timestamp guards prevent stale data from overwriting fresh online state.
Flushing Redis causes cold-start null spikes and breaks live inference.

options.text: Disable TTLs on all online keys
options.feedback: Disabling TTLs does not stop an older backfill write from overwriting a newer value.

_recommendedProblem.title: Active-Active Multi-Master Split-Brain Recovery
_recommendedProblem.prompt: Redesign an active-active multi-master relational replication pipeline between us-east-1 and eu-west-1 (6,000 writes/sec, 85 ms WAN RTT, < 15 ms p99 local commit) so a 9-minute transatlantic partition and 180-250 ms NTP clock skew never cause silent Last-Write-Wins (LWW) overwrites.
